title: PRD: Define automated degradation budgets and experimentation criteria for tail-latency incidents
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: A recent tail-latency incident (internal incident INC-2025-02-TL) exposed that our current PRD lacks quantifiable, automatable degradation budgets and a clear experimentation gating process. Engineering's emergency fallback behavior (hard model downgrade + tenant-wide throttles) reduced P99 latency but caused unacceptable quality regressions for high-value tenants. Postmortem recommended converting runbook actions into PRD-level, verifiable contracts so runtime teams can automate safe degradations and product teams can run controlled experiments.

This PRD scopes a set of requirements that translate incident actions into product-grade specifications: (1) a data model and API for per-tenant/per-route degradation budgets, (2) an observability/alerting contract (metrics + synthetic checks) that will trigger automated, gradual degradations, (3) an experimentation and canary strategy to validate degradations do not regress quality beyond agreed thresholds, and (4) UI surfaces and audit logs in Console to manage budgets and view historical degradations.

Out of scope: billing model changes, long-term pricing adjustments, and non-inference control plane redesigns. We do include integration obligations for Dedicated and Private (VPC) deployments where tenants want on-prem budget controls.

Why this matters: Turning qualitative incident runbook steps into machine-readable, testable specifications reduces Toil during incidents, makes rollbacks deterministic, and enables product teams to weigh quality vs availability trade-offs with measurable experiments.
acceptance_criteria: SLOs and degradation budgets defined as machine-readable objects: must include budget window, allowed error spike % (for quality), allowed latency increase %, and maximum duration
Runtime implements a configurable API (runtime-config/v1/degradation-budgets) supporting per-tenant and per-route scope
Console UI: budget create/edit/list + visual history charting for last 90 days for each budget
Observability contract: synthetic canary checks (per-route) + signals exposed — p95,p99,p999 latency, tail decode token latency, error-rate, rollback-safe-quality-score

Automated gating: when synthetic checks cross thresholds for 3 consecutive windows, runtime triggers a staged degradation plan (step-down model variant, progressive throttling) documented in a generated runbook entry
Experimentation harness: ability to run canary degradations against X% of traffic with automatic rollback if quality delta > configured threshold
Auditability: every automatic or manual budget-triggered degradation is recorded with actor, timestamp, reason, and metrics snapshot
End-to-end tests: chaos simulation reproducing incident class triggers the budget -> degradation path and validates rollback within SLA
Customer opt-out: tenant-level flag to disable automated degradations with acceptance of higher operator intervention required
Security: budget API access follows RBAC and logs to existing audit logging pipeline
tasks: Draft PRD and internal engineering review notes
Align on metric definitions with SRE (p95/p99/p999, decode tail latency, quality score metric)
Create runtime design RFC (ENG) covering API schema and enforcement points
Design Console UX mockups and place in drive: /drive/redwood/product/degradation-budgets
Implement metrics and synthetic check scaffolding (SRE + Eng)
Runtime API implementation and integration tests
Build Console surfaces and hook audit logs
Run chaos experiments in staging to validate automations and rollback criteria
Update incident runbooks to reference new machine-readable budgets
decisions: Primary metric set chosen: p95, p99, p999 latency + decode token tail latency + error-rate + a composite quality delta computed by eval-run against saved prompt sets
Budget granularity: per-tenant -> per-application-route -> per-model-variant (allows inheritance and overrides)
Default policy: conservative staged degradation (model-variant step-down then throttling), not abrupt cutoffs
Experimentation approach: progressive canary (1%, 5%, 20%) with automatic rollback conditions rather than manual gating
Retention: budget change and audit history retained for 90 days in Console by default
notes: Trade-offs: smaller budgets reduce availability for edge traffic but protect output quality for core tenants; we chose staged degradation to prioritize quality preservation
Implementation complexity: runtime enforcement requires KV cache awareness to avoid cache poisoning during step-downs; Eng to provide kernel-switch safepoints
Cross-team impact: SRE, Runtime, Console, Security, and Solutions Engineering need alignment for defaults and customer opt-out workflows
